comments.text: It's a fallacy that you are actually saving money. You pay less now but you end up paying more for "replacements" over time. So that $100 microwave ends up being a better deal. It will probably last 25-30 years, whereas the $40 one will break in about 2-5 years, then you go out and get a new $45 one that will also last 2-5 years. By the time you get the third one, your at the same price as the $100 one and your now at 10 years in instead of the 25-30 years for the $100 one. I hate this throw away mentality. When I was a kid; my dad could fix most things. If he couldn't we could take it in for repairs. I have 6 broken portable fans, and can't find a single place in my area that does small appliance repairs. It's so wasteful.

comments.text:
Bailey I just watched this episode. And I must say the idea, of every customer taking one deodorant, to bring Walmart down, seems like a great idea. However, if you take a step back and think about the thousands of people that would be affected if Walmart shut down. The chain/domino effect that would start would have the potential to leave thousands without any income. Not saying Walmart is right in the way they treat their employees, or in the lack of livable wages. But, in this economy some income is definitely better than no income.  And it wouldn't just be the Walmart employees taking a hit but all of the distributors/manufactures that rely on Walmart bringing in probably their largest stream of revenue. If they lose that, layoffs and people being let go won't be far behind.
It does appear major conglomerates like Walmart are untouchable. And honestly with all the money the Waltons have stockpiled and the government bailouts and assistance even if Walmart were to shut down; I doubt you will be likely to see any of the Walton family applying for food stamps or section 8 any time soon. 
Unfortunately, they would go on being rich.
